title: Zustand basics: create, selectors, set, persist
objectives: Create a store with `create<T>()(…)` and use getState/setState outside React, including resets between tests
Predict what a selector does in Zustand v5: a primitive re-renders only when it changes, a fresh object loops unless wrapped in useShallow
Predict the one-level merge in set() and in persist's rehydration, and use functional set when an update builds on the current state
Configure persist with name and partialize, and keep persisted values out of the hydration render under SSR
Write a store hook on useSyncExternalStore that re-renders only when the selected slice changes

sources.title: Zustand docs: Prevent rerenders with useShallow

questions.prompt: What does `const useCounter = create<CounterState>()((set) => ({ … }))` give you?

options.text: A hook you call with a selector — and the store itself, via useCounter.getState() / setState() / getInitialState() / subscribe()
A provider component you must wrap the app in before any component can read the store
A React Context object, which you read with useContext
A store class you instantiate once per component

questions.explanation: `create` returns a hook that is *also* the store: `useCounter(selector)` inside React, `useCounter.getState()` outside it. No provider is needed — the store is a module-level singleton, which is exactly why it's app-lifetime state (and why tests must reset it).

questions.prompt: In Zustand v5 a component needs both `count` and `name`. Which call re-renders it only when one of them changes?

options.text: `useStore(useShallow((s) => ({ count: s.count, name: s.name })))`
`useStore((s) => ({ count: s.count, name: s.name }))`
`const { count, name } = useStore()`
`useStore((s) => ({ count: s.count, name: s.name }))` in a component wrapped in `React.memo`

questions.explanation: `useShallow` remembers the previous object and hands it back while `count` and `name` are shallow-equal, so the snapshot only changes when one of them does (two atomic selectors, `useStore((s) => s.count)` and `useStore((s) => s.name)`, work too). The bare object selector builds a new object on every call; React's `useSyncExternalStore` compares snapshots with `Object.is`, sees a change on every check, and in v5 re-renders until "Maximum update depth exceeded" — in v4 it re-rendered on every store change instead. No selector at all returns the whole state object, which is new after every `set`, so the component re-renders on any change. `React.memo` only compares props; it has no say over a store subscription, so it can't stop the loop.

questions.prompt: State is `{ filters: { status: "open", page: 2 } }` and you call `set({ filters: { status: "closed" } })`. What is `filters` afterwards?

options.text: { status: "closed" } — page is gone, because the merge is only one level deep
{ status: "closed", page: 2 } — set deep-merges nested objects
Zustand throws, because partial updates must include every nested key
Unchanged — you must use the functional form to update anything

questions.explanation: `set` shallow-merges at the top level only, so a nested object is replaced wholesale and `page` is lost. Spread it yourself: `set((s) => ({ filters: { ...s.filters, status: "closed" } }))`.

questions.prompt: When does `set({ count: count + 1 })` lose an update that `set((s) => ({ count: s.count + 1 }))` would not?

options.text: When `count` was read earlier — selected during the last render, or read before an `await` — so it can be older than the store's state
When two `set` calls run close together — `set` is batched, so the object form is computed before the earlier update applies
Always; the object form is deprecated
Only when the state has nested objects

questions.explanation: Zustand's `set` is synchronous: the store holds the new state before `set` returns, so `set((s) => …)` receives exactly what `getState()` would at that moment — there's no queue like `useState`'s for the function form to get ahead of. The risk is a value captured *before* the write: a `count` selected during the last render (two `useCounter.setState({ count: count + 1 })` calls in one click handler both write the same number), or a `getState()` taken before an `await` (two overlapping calls both start from the old value). The function form — or `get()` at the moment you write — always starts from the current state. Nested objects are a separate rule (the one-level merge), and the object form isn't deprecated: `set({ theme })` is fine when the new value doesn't depend on the old one.

questions.prompt: Why does a persisted store usually need `partialize`?

options.text: To choose which state is durable — keeping ephemeral, derived, or sensitive fields out of storage (and out of future migrations)
To stop the store's action functions from being persisted as junk keys that shadow the real ones
It's required; persist throws without it
To encrypt the persisted payload

questions.explanation: `persist` serializes the whole state by default, so without `partialize` you also write fields you never wanted on disk: a half-finished draft, something derived you should recompute, a user's email. Note what `partialize` is *not* for — stripping actions. JSON serialization drops function values, and rehydration shallow-merges the persisted object over the initializer, so your actions survive either way. `partialize: (s) => ({ theme: s.theme })` also shrinks the shape a future `migrate` has to handle.

questions.prompt: A Next.js page renders `useSettings.persist?.hasHydrated() ? useSettings.getState().theme : "system"` from a store persisted to `localStorage` (the `?.` is needed: on the server there is no storage, so `persist` never attaches `useSettings.persist`). The server rendered `system`; the saved theme is `dark`. What happens on the client's first render?

options.text: It renders `dark` and React reports a hydration mismatch: with `localStorage`, `persist` hydrated when the store was created, so `hasHydrated()` is already `true`
It renders `system`, then `dark` once the storage read finishes — the gate works
It renders `system` and never updates, because `hasHydrated()` isn't reactive
It renders `dark` with no error: React patches a text difference during hydration and moves on

questions.explanation: The persist docs say it outright: with synchronous storage the store is already hydrated at its creation — before React renders anything. So on the client `hasHydrated()` is `true` and `getState().theme` is `dark` on the very first render, while the server's HTML says `system`. `hasHydrated()` really is a non-reactive getter, but that doesn't matter here: it's already true. Only async storage (IndexedDB, AsyncStorage) hydrates later, in a microtask. Nor does React quietly patch the difference: React 19 reports "Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client" and re-renders that part of the tree on the client. The server side is fine only because of the `?.`: with no `window.localStorage` there, `persist` runs without storage, keeps the initial state and never attaches its `persist` API, so an unguarded `useSettings.persist.hasHydrated()` would crash the server render with a TypeError. What works is a gate that shows the server's default until after mount: a mounted flag (this app's `useMounted()` in `lib/use-mounted.ts`), or `skipHydration: true` plus `useSettings.persist.rehydrate()` in an effect.

questions.prompt: Two tests in one file interfere: the second starts with the count the first left behind. What's the fix?

options.text: Put the store back with `useCounter.setState(useCounter.getInitialState(), true)` between tests — by hand, or for every store at once with the official guide's `__mocks__/zustand.ts`
Nothing to fix — Vitest and Jest give each test a fresh copy of every module
Call `useCounter.setState({})` in `beforeEach` — an empty object clears the state
Wrap each test in a store provider

questions.explanation: A module-level store is created once per module registry, and both Vitest and Jest keep one registry per test *file* — so every test in the file shares it. Reset it between tests: `getInitialState()` returns what the initializer produced, and the `true` flag replaces the state instead of merging, so nothing from the previous test survives. Zustand's testing guide does this for every store at once: a shared `__mocks__/zustand.ts` wraps `create`, records each store's initial state, and resets them all after each test. `setState({})` merges an empty object — it changes nothing. And a store from `create` has no provider to wrap.

prompts.prompt: Create a counter store whose increment reads the previous value.
prompts.explanation: `create` builds the hook/store from an initializer that receives `set`. Write it curried — `create<T>()(…)` — as Zustand's TypeScript guide recommends whenever you annotate the state type. The function form of `set` builds the next count from the store's current state, so an increment never starts from a stale copy.

prompts.prompt: Subscribe to just the count, so unrelated store changes don't re-render this component.
prompts.explanation: An atomic selector returns a primitive, so `Object.is` can tell whether it actually changed. Calling `useCounter()` with no selector subscribes to the whole state and re-renders on every change.

prompts.prompt: Read and write the store from plain, non-React code (a test, an event handler in a module).
prompts.explanation: The hook is also the store object: `getState()` reads the current state (actions included) and `setState()` writes it — no component, no renderer. This is what makes a Zustand store straightforward to unit test.

prompts.prompt: Persist only the theme under a named storage key.
prompts.explanation: `persist` wraps the initializer; `name` is the storage key and `partialize` picks which state gets written — here only `theme`. It isn't there to strip actions: JSON drops functions anyway, and rehydration merges the stored object over the initializer, so `setTheme` survives either way. The curried `create<Settings>()( … )` matters here: with a middleware wrapping the initializer, `create<Settings>(…)` doesn't type-check.

code: const useStore = create((set) => ({ count: 0, name: "Ana", setName: (name) => set({ name }) }));
snippets.question: The app runs Zustand v5. What happens when CountLabel mounts?
snippets.answer: It never settles: it re-renders until React throws "Maximum update depth exceeded"
snippets.explanation: v5's hook is `useSyncExternalStore` with `() => selector(getState())` as the snapshot. React re-renders whenever the snapshot differs by `Object.is` from the last one, and it re-reads the snapshot after rendering to check — `({ count: s.count })` is a new object every time, so it never stops. Nothing in the store has to change; mounting is enough. In development React first warns "The result of getSnapshot should be cached". If you answered "it renders, then re-renders on every store change", that was v4 (and is still `createWithEqualityFn` from `zustand/traditional`). Fix: `useStore((s) => s.count)`, or `useShallow` when you need an object.

code: // In the browser. Last month's release saved this under "settings":
// This release adds a nested default:
snippets.question: A returning user loads this release. What is logged?
snippets.explanation: Rehydration merges the stored state over the initial state with a shallow spread (`{ ...current, ...persisted }`) — the same one-level rule as `set`. The stored `prefs` replaces the whole default `prefs`, so `fontSize` is missing for every user who saved settings before this release, while new users get 16 — which is why it slips through testing. (It's logged already hydrated because `localStorage` is synchronous: persist hydrates when the store is created.) Fix it with a deep `merge` option, or bump `version` and fill the new field in `migrate`.

code: await saveToServer(); // any await: a fetch, a timer
// count is 0. A double-click starts two addOne() calls that overlap.
snippets.question: What is logged — and what would `useCart.setState((s) => ({ count: s.count + 1 }))` after the await give?
snippets.explanation: Each call reads `count === 0`, then pauses at `await` before writing, so both write `0 + 1` and one increment is lost. `setState` itself is synchronous — two clicks with no `await` between read and write would each see the fresh state and give 2 — so the bug lives in the gap between the read and the write. The function form reads the store's state at the moment it writes, after the `await`, so the second call starts from 1. Same root cause as a value selected during the last render: anything you read before the write can be stale by the time you write.
